name: Judas Iscariot
bio: Judas Iscariot was one of the twelve apostles Jesus named and sent out with authority to heal and cast out demons, instructed to go first to Israel rather than Gentiles or Samaritans; he is identified here as the one who would later betray Jesus (Matthew 10:1-5). His betrayal is told in detail in the chapters ahead. Shortly before the Passover, Judas went to the chief priests and agreed to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver, then watched for an opportunity to hand him over (Matthew 26:14-16). At the Last Supper, Jesus identified Judas as his betrayer when Judas asked directly. In Gethsemane, Judas led an armed crowd to Jesus and identified him with a kiss, completing the betrayal (Matthew 26:20-25, 47-50). Seized with remorse after Jesus was condemned, Judas tried to return the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests, declaring he had betrayed innocent blood; when they refused to take the money back, he threw it down in the temple and went out and hanged himself. The chief priests used the silver to buy a potter's field as a burial ground for strangers, fulfilling a prophecy Matthew attributes to Jeremiah the prophet (Matthew 27:3-10). John's Gospel identifies him as the son of Simon, and notes that even at the height of his popularity, Jesus knew Judas did not truly believe and would betray him (John 6:70-71). At the dinner in Bethany, Judas objected that Mary's costly ointment should have been sold to help the poor; John notes this was not out of real concern for the poor but because Judas, who kept the disciples' money bag, was a thief (John 12:4-6). Peter later recounted Judas's end differently, telling the gathered believers that Judas, having bought a field with his reward for the betrayal, fell headlong and burst open there, so that the field became known as Aceldama, "the field of blood" (Acts 1:16-19).
